evidence_quotes.quote: A study was undertaken in ten Asian countries to investigate the roles of and interaction between the public sector, private entities and civil society in serving the urban poor with water supply, sanitation and solid waste management.
Manila Water has a programme which relaxes some application requirements and so makes improved connections possible.
This approach waives the land title requirement and allows payment of connection fees by installment over a period of 6 or 12 months, in some cases extended to 24 months.
As a result, the community cannot take advantage of the cheaper bulk water rates and suffer as a consequence from the effects of rising block tariffs.

The pre-selection of case studies to ensure some level of coverage of the most common alternatives, including a sample of partnerships known to have failed, leads us to a qualitative understanding of strengths and weaknesses rather than any objective analysis of results of a random sample.

In western Jakarta, Palyja (the new private utility) are extending the distribution network to low-income people. These customers pay the connection fee in 12 monthly instalments of $0.71 which is added to their consumption tariff.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water supply and sanitation service access (alongside solid waste management) for low-income urban slum and squatter residents across 10 Asian and Pacific countries.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, it examines institutional, contractual, and governance arrangements (public-private-community partnerships, concessions, BOTs, and NGO intermediary agreements). Under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly examines utility ownership/contractual coverage obligations and concrete access-governing rules, including relaxation of utility application requirements, waiver of land title requirements (Maynilad's Bayan Tubig programme), installment rules for connection fees (Manila and Jakarta), tariff classification and rising block tariff penalties on community master meters, user-fee exemptions for destitute/disabled sanitation users (Sulabh), and regulatory forbearance toward illegal squatter connections.
criterion_notes.c3: Reports a comparative qualitative empirical study of 20 purposively selected case studies conducted in 2001 across 10 countries (ADB RETA 5926), drawing on fieldwork by country-based researchers including focus group discussions with low-income slum residents, customer satisfaction interviews, and operator interviews. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with identifiable data and methods are eligible even without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service-access outcomes including new household, group, and community water connections, access to community toilet blocks, water expenditures and affordability relative to informal vendors, collection and queuing time, 24-hour supply continuity, water pressure, and household water consumption.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (urban poor/slum households and communities across 20 partnership cases in 10 Asian/Pacific countries), exposure (PPP/NGO contractual structures and tenure, application, connection-fee, and tariff rules), outcome (connections, affordability, time savings, continuity, quantity), and study design (purposive comparative qualitative multiple-case study) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Comparative qualitative multiple-case study (20 purposively selected case studies with focus group discussions and interviews)
country: Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines, Vanuatu, Viet Nam
population_and_sample: Low-income urban slum and squatter residents and service partnerships across 20 purposively selected case studies in 10 Asian and Pacific countries (undertaken in 2001; household, community, and utility/partnership levels)
exposure: Public-private-community partnership contractual models (concessions, leases, BOTs, NGO intermediary agreements) and specific rule-type mechanisms governing access (waiver of land title and application requirements, connection-fee installment schedules, residential rising block tariff rules vs bulk rates, user-fee waivers for destitute/disabled users, and non-enforcement against illegal squatter connections)
outcome: Household, group, and community water and sanitation connections, water and sanitation affordability/expenditures, collection and queuing time, service continuity (24-hour supply), pressure, and household consumption quantity
rationale: This comparative qualitative study of 20 infrastructure partnership case studies in 10 Asian/Pacific countries (undertaken in 2001 with focus group discussions and interviews in low-income slums) meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Beyond institutional/contractual partnership forms (concessions, NGO agreements, leases, BOTs), it empirically examines concrete rule-type access mechanisms—including waivers of land-title and application requirements, connection-fee installment rules, rising block tariff penalties on community master connections, and fee waivers for destitute users—and links them to household connection, affordability, collection time, continuity, and consumption outcomes.
